theorem.title: Lemma — Noetherian local ring Noetherian

conclusions: A reduced, locally Noetherian singleton algebraic space $Z$ is regular.
hypotheses: Let $S$ be a scheme and $X$ an algebraic space over $S$. Write $|X|$ for its underlying topological space, obtained from the equivalence classes of morphisms $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ from spectra of fields. The fibre product of algebraic spaces is understood in the category of algebraic spaces. For an étale presentation $U\to X$ by a scheme, $R=U\times_XU$ is its groupoid of arrows with projections $s,t:R\rightrightarrows U$. A morphism is representable if every base change along a map from a scheme has scheme source.

For $x\in|X|$, condition $(\alpha)_x$ means every affine étale morphism $U\to X$ has only finitely many points over $x$. Condition $(\beta)_x$ means there is a monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ representing $x$. Condition $(\gamma)_x$ means there is a quasi-compact monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ representing $x$, equivalently for every affine étale $U\to X$ both fibres over $x$ of $|U|\to|X|$ and $|U\times_XU|\to|X|$ are finite. The conditions $(\alpha),(\beta),(\gamma)$ mean the corresponding pointwise property holds at every $x$.

An algebraic space $X$ is *decent* when it satisfies $(\gamma)$, equivalently every point $x$ can be represented by a quasi-compact monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)\to X$. It is *reasonable* when it satisfies $(\delta)$, equivalently the fibres of every affine étale presentation $U\to X$ are universally bounded. It is *very reasonable* when it satisfies $(\epsilon)$, equivalently it has a Zariski-local quasi-compact surjective étale cover by schemes. The implications scheme or quasi-separated $\Rightarrow$ very reasonable $\Rightarrow$ reasonable $\Rightarrow$ decent hold.

A *residual space* $Z_x\to X$ at $x\in|X|$ is the unique monomorphism from a reduced locally Noetherian algebraic space with singleton underlying topology whose image is $x$ and which is universal among morphisms of such spaces into $X$ representing $x$. A space is *locally separated* if its diagonal is an immersion; it is quasi-separated if its diagonal is quasi-compact and quasi-separated. A locally Noetherian algebraic space is one with an étale cover by locally Noetherian schemes.

conclusions: The local rings of X are UFDs iff X is normal and the canonical $\operatorname{Pic}(X)\to\operatorname{Cl}(X)$ is surjective.

theorem.statement:
For a locally Noetherian integral scheme X write $R(X)$ for its function field. A prime divisor is an integral codimension-one closed subscheme; $\operatorname{Div}(X)$ consists of locally finite integer sums of them. At its generic point $\xi$, write $\operatorname{ord}_Z(a/b)=\operatorname{length}(\mathcal O_{X,\xi}/a)-\operatorname{length}(\mathcal O_{X,\xi}/b)$ for nonzero local a,b. For a meromorphic line section s use $a/b=s/e$ with e a local generator of the line bundle; define $\operatorname{div}_{\mathcal L}(s)=\sum_Z\operatorname{ord}_{Z,\mathcal L}(s)[Z]$. Principal divisors are $\operatorname{div}_X(f)$ for $f\in R(X)^*$; $\operatorname{Cl}(X)$ is Div modulo principal divisors. The canonical map $\operatorname{Pic}(X)\to\operatorname{Cl}(X)$ sends a line bundle to the class of its nonzero meromorphic section. Let $X$ be a locally Noetherian integral scheme. Consider the map
(\ref{equation-c1}) $\Pic(X) \to \text{Cl}(X)$.
The following are equivalent
\begin{enumerate}
\item the local rings of $X$ are UFDs, and
\item $X$ is normal and $\Pic(X) \to \text{Cl}(X)$
is surjective.
\end{enumerate}
In this case $\Pic(X) \to \text{Cl}(X)$ is an isomorphism.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a category. For every $U\in\Ob(\mathcal C)$ write $h_U(T)=\Mor_{\mathcal C}(T,U)$, a contravariant functor into sets, and let $h:\mathcal C\to\mathrm{PSh}(\mathcal C)$ send $U$ to $h_U$ and a morphism to postcomposition.

given any contravariant functor $F$ and any object

$$

\quad

theorem.statement:

For $f:X\to Y$ in this category, choose a *compactification* $X\xrightarrow{j}\overline X\xrightarrow{\bar f}Y$, with $j$ an open immersion and $\bar f$ proper. Since $\overline X,Y$ are qcqs, the derived pushforward $R\bar f_*:D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_{\bar X})\to D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_Y)$ has a right adjoint $a_{\bar f}$. Define the *upper-shriek* functor $f^!:D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}^+(\mathcal O_Y)\to D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}^+(\mathcal O_X)$ by $f^!(K)=j^*a_{\bar f}(K)$, with the canonical identifications between compactifications. \[
p^!(-)\cong Lp^*(-)[1]:D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}^+(\mathcal O_Y)\to D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}^+(\mathcal O_{\mathbf A^1_Y}).
\]

A $q$-cycle on $T$ is a locally finite integral linear combination of integral closed subschemes of $\delta$-dimension $q$; $Z_q(T)$ is the group of these cycles. For a closed subscheme $W$ of dimension at most $q$, $[W]_q$ is the sum of the $q$-dimensional components weighted by generic-point length multiplicities. The Chow group $\mathrm{CH}_q(T)$ is $Z_q(T)$ modulo rational equivalence generated by locally finite principal divisors on integral closed subschemes of dimension $q+1$.

For a morphism $f:X\to Y$ and integer $p$, a bivariant class $c\in A^p(X\to Y)$ is a collection of homomorphisms $c_T:\mathrm{CH}_q(T)\to\mathrm{CH}_{q-p}(X\times_YT)$ indexed by $T\to Y$ and $q$, satisfying: (i) for proper $h:T'\to T$, $c_T(h_*\beta)=h_{X,*}c_{T'}(\beta)$; (ii) for flat $h$ of fixed relative dimension, $c_{T'}(h^*\alpha)=h_X^*c_T(\alpha)$; (iii) for $i:E\hookrightarrow T$ the zero scheme of a section of an invertible sheaf, $c_E(i^*\alpha)=i_X^*c_T(\alpha)$, with $h_X,i_X$ the base changes. The derived category $D(\mathcal O_X)$ is the localization of complexes of $\mathcal O_X$-modules at quasi-isomorphisms. A perfect object is locally quasi-isomorphic to a bounded complex of finite locally free modules. A locally bounded complex is bounded in cohomological degrees locally on $X$; derived pullback is denoted $Lf^*$ and derived tensor product $\otimes^{\mathbf L}$.

For a bounded complex of finite locally free $\mathcal E^\bullet$, put $c(\mathcal E^\bullet)=\prod_n c(\mathcal E^n)^{(-1)^n}$ (formal multiplication and inversion in $\prod_{p\ge0}A^p(X)$), $P_p(\mathcal E^\bullet)=\sum_n(-1)^n P_p(\mathcal E^n)$ and $\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal E^\bullet)=\sum_n(-1)^n\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal E^n)$. For a locally bounded complex use this construction on open-and-closed pieces where the terms have constant rank and finitely many are nonzero. For an $\mathcal O_X$-module F, $F^*=\mathcal Hom(F,\mathcal O_X)$ and reflexive means the evaluation map $F\to F^{**}$ is an isomorphism. The rank-one reflexive group law is $[F][G]=[(F\otimes G)^{**}]$. For a locally Noetherian integral scheme X write $R(X)$ for its function field. conclusions: A covering of T in Sch_etale exists which refines {T_i→T}.

Let $\Sch_\etale$ be a big \'etale site as in
Definition \ref{definition-big-etale-site}.
Let $T \in \Ob(\Sch_\etale)$.
Let $\{T_i \to T\}_{i \in I}$ be an arbitrary \'etale covering of $T$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item There exists a covering $\{U_j \to T\}_{j \in J}$ of $T$ in the site
$\Sch_\etale$ which refines $\{T_i \to T\}_{i \in I}$.

\item If $\{T_i \to T\}_{i \in I}$ is a Zariski covering, then

Two families over the same target are tautologically equivalent when there are maps between their index sets in both directions and isomorphisms over the target from each source object to the corresponding source object in the other family.

A closed point $x$ of a one-dimensional locally finite type $k$-scheme $X$ is a *node* if for an algebraic closure $\bar k$ some point $\bar x$ of $X_{\bar k}$ over $x$ has completed local ring $\bar k[[u,v]]/(uv)$. theorem.statement:
For functions $f_1,\ldots,f_r$ on a ringed space, regular means successive multiplication maps on $\mathcal O/(f_1,\ldots,f_{i-1})$ are injective; no nonzero-final-quotient condition is imposed here. Koszul-regular means the Koszul complex has zero homology in every positive degree; $H_1$-regular means its degree-one homology vanishes; quasi-regular means, with $\mathcal J=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ the ideal sheaf generated by the sequence, that $(\mathcal O/\mathcal J)[T_1,\ldots,T_r]\to\bigoplus_{n\geq0}\mathcal J^n/\mathcal J^{n+1}$ is an isomorphism, sending $T_i$ to $f_i$ modulo $\mathcal J^2$. An ideal sheaf is of a given type if near each point of $\operatorname{Supp}(\mathcal O/\mathcal J)$ it admits generators of that type. For a ring regular sequence one additionally requires the final quotient nonzero. An immersion is of a given type when its defining ideal on an open where it is closed is of that type. $H_1$-regular, quasi-regular) immersion. Let $X' \to X$ be a flat
morphism. Then the base change $i' : Z \times_X X' \to X'$
is a regular (resp.\ Koszul-regular,
$H_1$-regular, quasi-regular) immersion.

hypotheses: Let $S$ be a scheme and $X$ an algebraic space over $S$. Write $|X|$ for its underlying topological space, obtained from the equivalence classes of morphisms $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ from spectra of fields. The fibre product of algebraic spaces is understood in the category of algebraic spaces. For an étale presentation $U\to X$ by a scheme, $R=U\times_XU$ is its groupoid of arrows with projections $s,t:R\rightrightarrows U$. A morphism is representable if every base change along a map from a scheme has scheme source.

For $x\in|X|$, condition $(\alpha)_x$ means every affine étale morphism $U\to X$ has only finitely many points over $x$. Condition $(\beta)_x$ means there is a monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ representing $x$. Condition $(\gamma)_x$ means there is a quasi-compact monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ representing $x$, equivalently for every affine étale $U\to X$ both fibres over $x$ of $|U|\to|X|$ and $|U\times_XU|\to|X|$ are finite. The conditions $(\alpha),(\beta),(\gamma)$ mean the corresponding pointwise property holds at every $x$.

For points $a,b$ of a topological space, $b\leadsto a$ means $a\in\overline{\{b\}}$, i.e., $a$ is a specialization of $b$. The space is $T_0$ (Kolmogorov) when distinct points have distinct closures, and sober when every irreducible closed subset has exactly one generic point. A subset is locally constructible if its intersection with every quasi-compact open subset is a finite union of locally closed subsets. An algebraic space has a locally constructible subset in the étale sense when its inverse image in every étale scheme chart is locally constructible.

An algebraic space $X$ is *decent* when it satisfies $(\gamma)$, equivalently every point $x$ can be represented by a quasi-compact monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)\to X$. It is *reasonable* when it satisfies $(\delta)$, equivalently the fibres of every affine étale presentation $U\to X$ are universally bounded. It is *very reasonable* when it satisfies $(\epsilon)$, equivalently it has a Zariski-local quasi-compact surjective étale cover by schemes. The implications scheme or quasi-separated $\Rightarrow$ very reasonable $\Rightarrow$ reasonable $\Rightarrow$ decent hold.

A stack in groupoids additionally satisfies effective descent for objects and the sheaf condition for isomorphisms under fppf covers. A representable fibred groupoid is the one associated to an algebraic space. All fibre products of such fibred groupoids are $2$-fibre products (objects include comparison isomorphisms).

A morphism $p:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y$ of fibred groupoids is representable by algebraic spaces if, for every scheme $T$ and $y\in\mathcal Y(T)$, the $2$-fibre product $T\times_{\mathcal Y}\mathcal X$ is represented by an algebraic space $X_y$ over $T$. Fix a base scheme $S$ and the big fppf site $(\operatorname{Sch}/S)_{\mathrm{fppf}}$. A category fibred in groupoids over this site assigns a groupoid of objects over each $S$-scheme, with pullback functors and coherent comparison isomorphisms. A stack in groupoids additionally satisfies effective descent for objects and the sheaf condition for isomorphisms under fppf covers. A representable fibred groupoid is the one associated to an algebraic space. All fibre products of such fibred groupoids are $2$-fibre products (objects include comparison isomorphisms).

A morphism $p:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y$ of fibred groupoids is representable by algebraic spaces if, for every scheme $T$ and $y\in\mathcal Y(T)$, the $2$-fibre product $T\times_{\mathcal Y}\mathcal X$ is represented by an algebraic space $X_y$ over $T$. A representable morphism has a property such as étale, smooth, flat, locally of finite presentation, or surjective when every such $X_y\to T$ has that property. The diagonal $\Delta_\mathcal X:\mathcal X\to\mathcal X\times\mathcal X$ sends $x$ to $(x,x)$; its diagonal $\Delta_\Delta$ maps $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal X\times_{\mathcal X\times\mathcal X}\mathcal X$ and corresponds to the identity automorphism in the inertia groupoid. An algebraic stack is an fppf stack in groupoids with representable diagonal and a smooth surjective atlas by a scheme.

A morphism $p:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y$ is limit preserving on objects if, whenever an affine scheme $U=\varprojlim_i U_i$ is an inverse limit of affine $S$-schemes, $y_i\in\mathcal Y(U_i)$, $x\in\mathcal X(U)$, and an isomorphism $\gamma:p(x)\xrightarrow{\sim}y_i|_U$ are given, then for some $j\ge i$ there exist $x_j\in\mathcal X(U_j)$, an isomorphism $\beta:x_j|_U\xrightarrow{\sim}x$, and an isomorphism $\gamma_j:p(x_j)\xrightarrow{\sim}y_i|_{U_j}$ whose pullback to $U$ agrees with $\gamma$ after $p(\beta)$.

Let $p : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}$ be a $1$-morphism of categories
fibred in groupoids over $(\operatorname{Sch}/S)_{fppf}$. If $p$ is
representable by algebraic spaces, then the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $p$ is limit preserving on objects, and
\item $p$ is locally of finite presentation (meaning that all algebraic-space base changes have this property).
\end{enumerate}

theorem.title: Lemma — Fibre products etale

conclusions: $\mathcal J$ is a finite type quasi-coherent ideal sheaf.
hypotheses: X is a scheme and $\mathcal J$ is an ideal sheaf that is regular, Koszul-regular, H1-regular, or quasi-regular.
theorem.statement:
For functions $f_1,\ldots,f_r$ on a ringed space, regular means successive multiplication maps on $\mathcal O/(f_1,\ldots,f_{i-1})$ are injective; no nonzero-final-quotient condition is imposed here. Koszul-regular means the Koszul complex has zero homology in every positive degree; $H_1$-regular means its degree-one homology vanishes; quasi-regular means, with $\mathcal J=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ the ideal sheaf generated by the sequence, that $(\mathcal O/\mathcal J)[T_1,\ldots,T_r]\to\bigoplus_{n\geq0}\mathcal J^n/\mathcal J^{n+1}$ is an isomorphism, sending $T_i$ to $f_i$ modulo $\mathcal J^2$. An ideal sheaf is of a given type if near each point of $\operatorname{Supp}(\mathcal O/\mathcal J)$ it admits generators of that type. For a ring regular sequence one additionally requires the final quotient nonzero. An immersion is of a given type when its defining ideal on an open where it is closed is of that type. Relative quasi/$H_1$-regular means also that its source is flat over the base. Any regular, Koszul-regular, $H_1$-regular, or quasi-regular sheaf
of ideals on a scheme is a finite type quasi-coherent sheaf of ideals.

A category fibred in groupoids over this site assigns a groupoid of objects over each $S$-scheme, with pullback functors and coherent comparison isomorphisms. A stack in groupoids additionally satisfies effective descent for objects and the sheaf condition for isomorphisms under fppf covers. A representable fibred groupoid is the one associated to an algebraic space. All fibre products of such fibred groupoids are $2$-fibre products (objects include comparison isomorphisms).

A morphism $p:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y$ of fibred groupoids is representable by algebraic spaces if, for every scheme $T$ and $y\in\mathcal Y(T)$, the $2$-fibre product $T\times_{\mathcal Y}\mathcal X$ is represented by an algebraic space $X_y$ over $T$. A representable morphism has a property such as étale, smooth, flat, locally of finite presentation, or surjective when every such $X_y\to T$ has that property. The diagonal $\Delta_\mathcal X:\mathcal X\to\mathcal X\times\mathcal X$ sends $x$ to $(x,x)$; its diagonal $\Delta_\Delta$ maps $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal X\times_{\mathcal X\times\mathcal X}\mathcal X$ and corresponds to the identity automorphism in the inertia groupoid. An algebraic stack is an fppf stack in groupoids with representable diagonal and a smooth surjective atlas by a scheme.

A morphism $F:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y$ of fppf stacks in groupoids is algebraic if for every scheme $T$ and every object $y\in\mathcal Y(T)$ the $2$-fibre product $T\times_{\mathcal Y}\mathcal X$ is an algebraic stack. This notion is broader than being representable by algebraic spaces.

conclusions: Coherent duality and biduality, with bounded-subcategory statements under qc.
hypotheses: X locally Noetherian, K dualizing (affine-locally from ring-theoretic dualizing complexes); X qc for boundedness claims.
theorem.statement: Here $D_{\mathrm{Coh}}(\mathcal O_X)$ denotes the full derived subcategory of complexes with coherent cohomology, and $D^{\pm},D^b$ denote bounded-below, bounded-above, and bounded derived subcategories. A *dualizing complex* over a Noetherian ring $A$ is a bounded complex with finitely generated cohomology, finite injective dimension, and a homothety quasi-isomorphism $A\simeq R\operatorname{Hom}_A(D,D)$. For a locally Noetherian scheme $X$, a complex $K\in D(\mathcal O_X)$ is *dualizing* if affine locally it is the sheafification of such a ring-theoretic dualizing complex. If $K$ is such a dualizing complex on $X$, then $K\in D_{\mathrm{Coh}}(\mathcal O_X)$ and the contravariant functor $\mathbb D_K(E)=R\mathcal Hom_{\mathcal O_X}(E,K)$ takes $D_{\mathrm{Coh}}(\mathcal O_X)$ to itself and is an anti-equivalence, with the natural biduality map $E\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb D_K\mathbb D_K(E)$ for every $E$ in this coherent-derived category. If $X$ is in addition quasi-compact, $\mathbb D_K$ exchanges $D_{\mathrm{Coh}}^{+}$ and $D_{\mathrm{Coh}}^{-}$ and restricts to an anti-equivalence of $D_{\mathrm{Coh}}^b$ with itself.

theorem.title: Lemma — Descending property finite type

conclusions: Deligne-pro-isomorphism characterized by I-adic cohomology pro-systems.
hypotheses: Noetherian open immersion, fixed ideal I cutting out complement, uniformly bounded inverse system K_n.
theorem.statement: For a Noetherian scheme $X$, open immersion $j:U\hookrightarrow X$, and coherent bounded complex $\mathcal F^\bullet$ on $X$, choose a quasi-coherent ideal $\mathcal I\subset\mathcal O_X$ whose vanishing set is $X\setminus U$. Define $K_n$ as the bounded coherent *subcomplex* with terms $\mathcal I^n\mathcal F^q$ and differentials induced by those of $\mathcal F^\bullet$. The inverse system $(K_n)_{n\ge1}$, with maps induced by $\mathcal I^{n+1}\mathcal F^\bullet\subseteq\mathcal I^n\mathcal F^\bullet$, is a *Deligne system* for $j$. Its restriction to $U$ is a constant system in $D_{\mathrm{Coh}}^b(\mathcal O_U)$ with value $K=\mathcal F^\bullet|_U$. A *pro-isomorphism* refers to isomorphism in $\operatorname{Pro}(D_{\mathrm{Coh}}^b(\mathcal O_X))$, whose Hom sets into a constant object $L$ are $\operatorname*{colim}_n\operatorname{Hom}_{D_{\mathrm{Coh}}^b(X)}(K_n,L)$. Fix a quasi-coherent ideal $\mathcal I\subseteq\mathcal O_X$ with $V(\mathcal I)=X\setminus U$. Let $(K_n)$ be an inverse system in $D_{\mathrm{Coh}}^b(\mathcal O_X)$ with a *uniform* cohomological amplitude $[a,b]$, i.e. $H^i(K_n)=0$ for all $n$ when $i\notin[a,b]$. Then the following are equivalent: (1) $(K_n)$ is pro-isomorphic to a Deligne system for $U\subseteq X$; (2) for every $p\in\mathbf Z$ there is a coherent $\mathcal O_X$-module $\mathcal F_p$ such that the inverse systems of coherent sheaves $(H^p(K_n))_n$ and $(\mathcal I^n\mathcal F_p)_n$ are isomorphic as pro-objects. This condition is independent of the choice of coherent $\mathcal F_p$ and only finitely many $p$ are nonzero due to $[a,b]$.

for $i > m + 1$, then $H^{m + 1}(K)$ is a finitely presented

\end{enumerate}

conclusions: For every $i\ge0$, $H^i_{\mathrm{Ab}(\mathcal C)}(\mathcal C,\mathcal F_{ab})\cong H^i_{\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O)}(\mathcal C,\mathcal F)$ as abelian groups.

theorem.statement:
Let $\mathcal F_{ab}$ denote the abelian sheaf underlying an $\mathcal O$-module $\mathcal F$. The two cohomology functors in the comparisons are the derived section functors on $\mathrm{Ab}(\mathcal C)$ and on $\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O)$, respectively; the underlying abelian groups are compared, even when module cohomology has additional scalar structure.

=
H^i(\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{F})

$$
H^i(U, \mathcal{F}_{ab})
=
H^i(U, \mathcal{F}).

$\textit{Ab}(\mathcal{C})$ and the right hand side
is cohomology computed in $\textit{Mod}(\mathcal{O})$.

theorem.title: Lemma — Tensor algebra permanence

conclusions: $P'_p(E \oplus F) = P'_p(E) + P'_p(F)$.
hypotheses: Let $S$ be a locally Noetherian universally catenary scheme equipped with a dimension function $\delta:S\to\mathbf Z$. For any $S$-scheme $T$ locally of finite type, write $\delta_T(t)=\delta(f(t))+\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(f(t))}\kappa(t)$; for integral closed $W\subset T$, let $\dim_\delta W=\delta_T(\eta_W)$.

A $q$-cycle on $T$ is a locally finite integral linear combination of integral closed subschemes of $\delta$-dimension $q$; $Z_q(T)$ is the group of these cycles. For a closed subscheme $W$ of dimension at most $q$, $[W]_q$ is the sum of the $q$-dimensional components weighted by generic-point length multiplicities. The Chow group $\mathrm{CH}_q(T)$ is $Z_q(T)$ modulo rational equivalence generated by locally finite principal divisors on integral closed subschemes of dimension $q+1$.

For a morphism $f:X\to Y$ and integer $p$, a bivariant class $c\in A^p(X\to Y)$ is a collection of homomorphisms $c_T:\mathrm{CH}_q(T)\to\mathrm{CH}_{q-p}(X\times_YT)$ indexed by $T\to Y$ and $q$, satisfying: (i) for proper $h:T'\to T$, $c_T(h_*\beta)=h_{X,*}c_{T'}(\beta)$; (ii) for flat $h$ of fixed relative dimension, $c_{T'}(h^*\alpha)=h_X^*c_T(\alpha)$; (iii) for $i:E\hookrightarrow T$ the zero scheme of a section of an invertible sheaf, $c_E(i^*\alpha)=i_X^*c_T(\alpha)$, with $h_X,i_X$ the base changes. Composition of families gives products $A^p(X\to Y)\times A^q(Y\to Z)\to A^{p+q}(X\to Z)$, and $A^*(X)=\bigoplus_pA^p(X\to X)$.

For a finite locally free sheaf $\mathcal E$ of rank $r$ on $X$, its operational Chern classes are $c_j(\mathcal E)\in A^j(X)$, with $c_0=1$, $c_j=0$ for $j>r$, and total class $c(\mathcal E)=\sum_jc_j(\mathcal E)$. For an integral closed $W\subset X$ of $\delta$-dimension $n$, the classes $c_j(\mathcal E|_W)\cap[W]$ in $\mathrm{CH}_{n-j}(W)$ are characterized via the projective bundle $\pi:\mathbf P(\mathcal E|_W)\to W$ with tautological quotient $\mathcal O(1)$ by $\sum_{i=0}^r(-1)^i c_1(\mathcal O(1))^i\cap\pi^*c_{r-i}=0$ with $c_0=[W]$. Extend to general cycles by sum and proper pushforward, then to Chow groups.

For a locally free $\mathcal E$ with formal Chern roots $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ (elementary symmetric polynomials equal to $c_i(\mathcal E)$), put $P_p(\mathcal E)=\sum_{j=1}^r x_j^p$, where $P_0=r$, and $\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal E)=\sum_{p\geq0}P_p(\mathcal E)/p!$. Each $P_p$ is the universal Newton polynomial in the Chern classes, and the degree-$p$ Chern character lies in $A^p(X)\otimes\mathbf Q$.

The derived category $D(\mathcal O_X)$ is the localization of complexes of $\mathcal O_X$-modules at quasi-isomorphisms. A perfect object is locally quasi-isomorphic to a bounded complex of finite locally free modules. A locally bounded complex is bounded in cohomological degrees locally on $X$; derived pullback is denoted $Lf^*$ and derived tensor product $\otimes^{\mathbf L}$.

For a bounded complex of finite locally free $\mathcal E^\bullet$, put $c(\mathcal E^\bullet)=\prod_n c(\mathcal E^n)^{(-1)^n}$ (formal multiplication and inversion in $\prod_{p\ge0}A^p(X)$), $P_p(\mathcal E^\bullet)=\sum_n(-1)^n P_p(\mathcal E^n)$ and $\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal E^\bullet)=\sum_n(-1)^n\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal E^n)$. For a locally bounded complex use this construction on open-and-closed pieces where the terms have constant rank and finitely many are nonzero. When the Chern classes of a perfect object $E$ are defined, these are the unique classes whose pullbacks to a suitable envelope agree with such a representing complex.

An envelope $f:Y\to X$ is a proper morphism such that every $x\in X$ has a preimage $y$ with $\kappa(y)\cong\kappa(x)$. We say Chern classes of a perfect object $E\in D(\mathcal O_X)$ are defined if an envelope $f:Y\to X$ exists such that $Lf^*E$ is represented by a locally bounded complex of finite locally free sheaves on $Y$.

For closed immersions $i_j:X_j\hookrightarrow X$ with $X=X_1\cup X_2$ set-theoretically and a perfect $E_2$ on $X_2$ whose Chern classes are defined, assume its restriction to $X_1\cap X_2$ is zero (for the power-sum class $P'_p(E_2)$), or a finite locally free sheaf of rank less than $p$ in degree zero (for the Chern class $c'_p(E_2)$). The canonical localized classes $P'_p(E_2),c'_p(E_2)\in A^p(X_2\to X)$ agree with $P_p(E_2),c_p(E_2)$ on cycles pushed from $X_2$ and vanish on cycles pushed from $X_1$, respectively, compatibly with locally finite type base changes.

Composition of families gives products $A^p(X\to Y)\times A^q(Y\to Z)\to A^{p+q}(X\to Z)$, and $A^*(X)=\bigoplus_pA^p(X\to X)$.

For a finite locally free sheaf $\mathcal E$ of rank $r$ on $X$, its operational Chern classes are $c_j(\mathcal E)\in A^j(X)$, with $c_0=1$, $c_j=0$ for $j>r$, and total class $c(\mathcal E)=\sum_jc_j(\mathcal E)$. For an integral closed $W\subset X$ of $\delta$-dimension $n$, the classes $c_j(\mathcal E|_W)\cap[W]$ in $\mathrm{CH}_{n-j}(W)$ are characterized via the projective bundle $\pi:\mathbf P(\mathcal E|_W)\to W$ with tautological quotient $\mathcal O(1)$ by $\sum_{i=0}^r(-1)^i c_1(\mathcal O(1))^i\cap\pi^*c_{r-i}=0$ with $c_0=[W]$. Extend to general cycles by sum and proper pushforward, then to Chow groups.

For a locally free $\mathcal E$ with formal Chern roots $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ (elementary symmetric polynomials equal to $c_i(\mathcal E)$), put $P_p(\mathcal E)=\sum_{j=1}^r x_j^p$, where $P_0=r$, and $\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal E)=\sum_{p\geq0}P_p(\mathcal E)/p!$. Each $P_p$ is the universal Newton polynomial in the Chern classes, and the degree-$p$ Chern character lies in $A^p(X)\otimes\mathbf Q$.

The derived category $D(\mathcal O_X)$ is the localization of complexes of $\mathcal O_X$-modules at quasi-isomorphisms. A perfect object is locally quasi-isomorphic to a bounded complex of finite locally free modules. A locally bounded complex is bounded in cohomological degrees locally on $X$; derived pullback is denoted $Lf^*$ and derived tensor product $\otimes^{\mathbf L}$.

For a bounded complex of finite locally free $\mathcal E^\bullet$, put $c(\mathcal E^\bullet)=\prod_n c(\mathcal E^n)^{(-1)^n}$ (formal multiplication and inversion in $\prod_{p\ge0}A^p(X)$), $P_p(\mathcal E^\bullet)=\sum_n(-1)^n P_p(\mathcal E^n)$ and $\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal E^\bullet)=\sum_n(-1)^n\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal E^n)$. For a locally bounded complex use this construction on open-and-closed pieces where the terms have constant rank and finitely many are nonzero. When the Chern classes of a perfect object $E$ are defined, these are the unique classes whose pullbacks to a suitable envelope agree with such a representing complex.

An envelope $f:Y\to X$ is a proper morphism such that every $x\in X$ has a preimage $y$ with $\kappa(y)\cong\kappa(x)$. We say Chern classes of a perfect object $E\in D(\mathcal O_X)$ are defined if an envelope $f:Y\to X$ exists such that $Lf^*E$ is represented by a locally bounded complex of finite locally free sheaves on $Y$.

For closed immersions $i_j:X_j\hookrightarrow X$ with $X=X_1\cup X_2$ set-theoretically and a perfect $E_2$ on $X_2$ whose Chern classes are defined, assume its restriction to $X_1\cap X_2$ is zero (for the power-sum class $P'_p(E_2)$), or a finite locally free sheaf of rank less than $p$ in degree zero (for the Chern class $c'_p(E_2)$). The canonical localized classes $P'_p(E_2),c'_p(E_2)\in A^p(X_2\to X)$ agree with $P_p(E_2),c_p(E_2)$ on cycles pushed from $X_2$ and vanish on cycles pushed from $X_1$, respectively, compatibly with locally finite type base changes.

\item Chern classes of $E$ and $F$ are defined,
\item the restrictions $E|_{X_1 \cap X_2}$ and $F|_{X_1 \cap X_2}$ are zero,

theorem.title: Lemma — Minimal support in ass

conclusions: For each simplicial object $U$, its face and degeneracy morphisms satisfy the five explicitly enumerated identities.
Conversely, any sequence of objects with face and degeneracy maps satisfying these five identities determines a unique simplicial object.
A simplicial morphism is exactly a degreewise family of arrows commuting with every face and degeneracy map.
hypotheses: Let $\mathcal C$ be a category.
theorem.statement:
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a category.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Given a simplicial object $U$ in $\mathcal{C}$
we obtain a sequence of objects $U_n = U([n])$ endowed
with the morphisms $d^n_j = U(\delta^n_j) : U_n \to U_{n-1}$ and
$s^n_j = U(\sigma^n_j) : U_n \to U_{n + 1}$. These morphisms satisfy the following simplicial identities:
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $0 \leq i < j \leq n + 1$, then
$d^n_i \circ d^{n + 1}_j = d^n_{j - 1} \circ d^{n + 1}_i$.
\item If $0 \leq i < j \leq n - 1$, then
$d^n_i \circ s^{n - 1}_j = s^{n - 2}_{j - 1} \circ d^{n - 1}_i$.
\item If $0 \leq j \leq n - 1$, then
$\text{id} = d^n_j \circ s^{n - 1}_j = d^n_{j + 1} \circ s^{n - 1}_j$.
\item If $0 < j + 1 < i \leq n$, then
$d^n_i \circ s^{n - 1}_j = s^{n - 2}_j \circ d^{n - 1}_{i - 1}$.
\item If $0 \leq i \leq j \leq n - 1$, then
$s^n_i \circ s^{n - 1}_j = s^n_{j + 1} \circ s^{n - 1}_i$.
\end{enumerate}
\item Conversely, given a sequence of objects $U_n$ and morphisms
$d^n_j$, $s^n_j$ satisfying (1)(a) -- (e) there exists a unique
simplicial object $U$ in $\mathcal{C}$ such that $U_n = U([n])$,
$d^n_j = U(\delta^n_j)$, and $s^n_j = U(\sigma^n_j)$.
\item A morphism between simplicial objects $U$ and $U'$
is given by a family of morphisms $U_n \to U'_n$ commuting
with the morphisms $d^n_j$ and $s^n_j$.
\end{enumerate}

For any proper such scheme $X$ with $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X)=k$, define its genus as $g(X)=\dim_k H^1(X,\mathcal O_X)$. If $X$ is one-dimensional, Cohen–Macaulay and equidimensional, its coherent dualizing module is $\omega_X=H^{-1}(f^!k)$ for $f:X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$; it is invertible when $X$ is Gorenstein.

For a Noetherian local $k$-algebra $(A,\mathfrak m,\kappa)$, the residue field extension is separable when $\kappa/k$ is separable. A nondegenerate binary quadratic form $q=au^2+buv+cv^2$ has invertible polar bilinear form (matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2a&b\\b&2c\end{pmatrix}$), and $\kappa[[u,v]]/(q)$ is the completed local model of a node. For a finitely presented module $M$ with presentation $R^m\to R^n\to M\to0$, its first Fitting ideal $\operatorname{Fitt}_1(M)$ is generated by the $(n-1)$-minors of the presenting matrix; for $M=\Omega_{X/k}$ this defines a closed subscheme of the singular locus. The number of geometric branches and $\delta$-invariant of a one-dimensional local ring are computed after normalization and separable closure of residue fields.

For a morphism of schemes $f:X\to S$, say *at worst nodal of relative dimension one* if $f$ is flat and locally of finite presentation and each nonempty geometric fibre is an equidimensional one-dimensional scheme with at-worst-nodal singularities. Equivalently $f$ is syntomic of relative dimension one and $\operatorname{Sing}(f)$, defined by the first Fitting ideal of $\Omega_{X/S}$, is unramified over $S$. Here syntomic means flat, locally of finite presentation, with local complete intersection fibres. This property is stable under base change and local for the étale topology on the source and fpqc topology on the target.

Let $f : X \to S$ be a morphism of schemes which is flat and
locally of finite presentation. Then there is a maximal open
subscheme $U \subset X$ such that $f|_U : U \to S$ is
at-worst-nodal of relative dimension $1$. Moreover, formation
of $U$ commutes with arbitrary base change.

For a Noetherian ring $A$, a *dualizing complex* means a bounded complex with coherent cohomology, finite injective dimension, and the canonical self-Hom identification $A\simeq R\operatorname{Hom}_A(D,D)$. For an ideal $I$, write $\widehat A^I=\varprojlim_n A/I^n$ for ordinary $I$-adic completion, and $(A^h,I^h)$ for henselization of the pair. The following types of rings have a dualizing complex:
\begin{enumerate}
\item fields,
\item Noetherian complete local rings,
\item $\mathbf{Z}$,
\item Dedekind domains,
\item any ring which is obtained from one of the rings above by
taking an algebra essentially of finite type, or by taking an
ideal-adic completion, or by taking a henselization, 
or by taking a strict henselization.
\end{enumerate}

The closure operations are taken successively where the resulting ring remains in the stated Noetherian category; no normalization choice is implied.

theorem.title: Lemma — Extensions of relative ringed topoi

conclusions: The two differ by tensoring with derived-invertible L.
hypotheses: A Noetherian, two dualizing complexes.
theorem.statement:
For a Noetherian ring $A$, let $D_{\rm Coh}(A)\subseteq D(A)$ be the full derived category of complexes with finitely generated cohomology in every degree. A *dualizing complex* $\omega_A^\bullet\in D(A)$ means a bounded complex with finite injective dimension and finitely generated cohomology such that the homothety map $A\to R\operatorname{Hom}_A(\omega_A^\bullet,\omega_A^\bullet)$ is an isomorphism. The functor $\mathbb D_A(K)=R\operatorname{Hom}_A(K,\omega_A^\bullet)$ is contravariant. If $\omega_A^\bullet$ and $(\omega'_A)^\bullet$ are two dualizing complexes, then there is a derived-invertible $L\in D(A)$, locally a shift of a line bundle, and an isomorphism
\[
(\omega'_A)^\bullet\simeq\omega_A^\bullet\otimes_A^{\mathbf L}L.
\]
Thus dualizing complexes are unique up to a derived-invertible twist, not generally an unshifted unique isomorphism.

theorem.title: Lemma — Directed colimit coherent

conclusions: $\omega_X$ is ample.
hypotheses: Let $k$ be a field. A proper curve over $k$ is a proper integral $k$-scheme of Krull dimension one; a proper $k$-scheme of dimension one need not be integral. For any proper such scheme $X$ with $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X)=k$, define its genus as $g(X)=\dim_k H^1(X,\mathcal O_X)$. If $X$ is one-dimensional, Cohen–Macaulay and equidimensional, its coherent dualizing module is $\omega_X=H^{-1}(f^!k)$ for $f:X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$; it is invertible when $X$ is Gorenstein.

A closed point $x$ of a one-dimensional locally finite type $k$-scheme $X$ is a *node* if for an algebraic closure $\bar k$ some point $\bar x$ of $X_{\bar k}$ over $x$ has completed local ring $\bar k[[u,v]]/(uv)$. All singularities of $X$ are *at worst nodal* if each closed point is smooth over $k$ or a node. Equivalently at a node $\kappa(x)/k$ is separable and $\widehat{\mathcal O}_{X,x}\cong\kappa(x)[[u,v]]/(au^2+buv+cv^2)$ for a nondegenerate binary quadratic form (whose discriminant is nonzero, including in characteristic $2$). Such curves are Gorenstein and geometrically reduced.

For a proper Cohen–Macaulay $k$-scheme $X$ of dimension one with $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X)=k$, put $\omega_X=H^{-1}(f^!k)$, $g=\dim_kH^1(X,\mathcal O_X)$, and for invertible $\mathcal L$ let $\deg(\mathcal L)=\chi(X,\mathcal L)-\chi(X,\mathcal O_X)$. If $X$ is Gorenstein, $\omega_X$ is an invertible sheaf of degree $2g-2$. For a zero-dimensional subscheme $Z\subset X$, $\deg(Z)=\dim_kH^0(Z,\mathcal O_Z)$.

For a proper $k$-scheme $X$ of dimension one with $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X)=k$ and at-worst-nodal singularities, a *rational bridge* $C\subset X$ is an integral irreducible component such that $X'$ (the scheme-theoretic closure of $X\setminus C$) is nonempty, $C$ has genus zero, and the scheme-theoretic intersection $C\cap X'$ is finite of degree two over $k'=H^0(C,\mathcal O_C)$ (either two $k'$-points or a degree-two separable point). Its contraction $c:X\to Y$ collapses $C$ to a point $y$ and is obtained from the pushout $Y=X'\amalg_{C\cap X'}\operatorname{Spec}k'$. It satisfies $c_*\mathcal O_X=\mathcal O_Y$ and $R^1c_*\mathcal O_X=0$; $Y$ remains at worst nodal. The genus of $Y$ equals that of $X$.

theorem.statement: Let $Y$ be quasi-compact and quasi-separated and $f:X\to Y$ proper, flat, and of finite presentation. Let $a_f$ be the right adjoint to $Rf_*$ on unbounded derived categories with quasi-coherent cohomology, and define the *relative dualizing complex* $\omega_{X/Y}^{\bullet}=a_f(\mathcal O_Y)\in D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_X)$. A complex in $D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_Y)$ is *supported on* a closed subset $T$ if every cohomology sheaf is zero on $Y\setminus T$. If $V\subseteq Y$ is open, $U=f^{-1}(V)$, and $j:V\hookrightarrow Y$, $j':U\hookrightarrow X$, the *restriction comparison* is the natural map $\rho_K:(j')^*a_f(K)\to a_{f|_U}(j^*K)$. Then (1) for every closed subset $T\subseteq Y$ and every $Q\in D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_Y)$ supported on $T$, $a_f(Q)$ is supported on $f^{-1}(T)$; and (2) for every quasi-compact open $V\subseteq Y$ and *every unbounded* $K\in D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_Y)$, the restriction comparison $\rho_K$ is an isomorphism. Both results hold without Noetherian assumptions on $Y$.

conclusions: The inverse system $M_n=H^p(\mathcal C,\mathcal F_n)$ satisfies the Mittag–Leffler condition.

theorem.statement:
An inverse system $(M_n)$ satisfies the Mittag–Leffler condition when, for every fixed $n$, the images of the transition maps $M_m\to M_n$ stabilize for all sufficiently large $m$. The graded ring $\bigoplus_{n\ge0}I^n/I^{n+1}$ is the associated graded ring of the $I$-adic filtration. For every $n$, set $N_n=\bigcap_{m\ge n}\mathrm{Im}(H^{p+1}(\mathcal C,I^n\mathcal F_{m+1})\to H^{p+1}(\mathcal C,I^n\mathcal F_{n+1}))$. The graded Noetherian/ACC hypothesis is on **$\bigoplus N_n$**, not on the larger direct sum of all degree-$p+1$ cohomology groups; the weaker image condition is essential.

Let $I$ be an ideal of a ring $A$. Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a site. Let
$$
\ldots \to \mathcal{F}_3 \to \mathcal{F}_2 \to \mathcal{F}_1
$$
be an inverse system of $A$-modules on $\mathcal{C}$
such that $\mathcal{F}_n = \mathcal{F}_{n + 1}/I^n\mathcal{F}_{n + 1}$.
Let $p \geq 0$. Given $n$ define
$$
N_n =
\bigcap\nolimits_{m \geq n}
\Im\left(
H^{p + 1}(\mathcal{C}, I^n\mathcal{F}_{m + 1}) \to
H^{p + 1}(\mathcal{C}, I^n\mathcal{F}_{n + 1})
\right)
$$
If $\bigoplus N_n$ satisfies the ascending chain condition as a graded
$\bigoplus_{n \geq 0} I^n/I^{n + 1}$-module, then the inverse system
$M_n = H^p(\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{F}_n)$ satisfies the Mittag-Leffler
condition\footnote{In fact, there exists
a $c \geq 0$ such that $\Im(M_n \to M_{n - c})$ is the stable image
for all $n \geq c$.}.

A category fibred in groupoids over this site assigns a groupoid of objects over each $S$-scheme, with pullback functors and coherent comparison isomorphisms. A stack in groupoids additionally satisfies effective descent for objects and the sheaf condition for isomorphisms under fppf covers. A representable fibred groupoid is the one associated to an algebraic space. All fibre products of such fibred groupoids are $2$-fibre products (objects include comparison isomorphisms).

A morphism $p:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y$ of fibred groupoids is representable by algebraic spaces if, for every scheme $T$ and $y\in\mathcal Y(T)$, the $2$-fibre product $T\times_{\mathcal Y}\mathcal X$ is represented by an algebraic space $X_y$ over $T$. A representable morphism has a property such as étale, smooth, flat, locally of finite presentation, or surjective when every such $X_y\to T$ has that property. The diagonal $\Delta_\mathcal X:\mathcal X\to\mathcal X\times\mathcal X$ sends $x$ to $(x,x)$; its diagonal $\Delta_\Delta$ maps $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal X\times_{\mathcal X\times\mathcal X}\mathcal X$ and corresponds to the identity automorphism in the inertia groupoid. An algebraic stack is an fppf stack in groupoids with representable diagonal and a smooth surjective atlas by a scheme.

conclusions: The upper-shriek functor for a closed immersion equals derived exact-support Hom.
hypotheses: i closed immersion in FTS_S; K bounded-below D_QCoh.
theorem.statement:
Fix a Noetherian base scheme $S$ and let $\mathrm{FTS}_S$ be the category of schemes $T$ with separated finite-type structure map $T\to S$, with $S$-morphisms. For $f:X\to Y$ in this category, choose a *compactification* $X\xrightarrow{j}\overline X\xrightarrow{\bar f}Y$, with $j$ an open immersion and $\bar f$ proper. Since $\overline X,Y$ are qcqs, the derived pushforward $R\bar f_*:D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_{\bar X})\to D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_Y)$ has a right adjoint $a_{\bar f}$. Define the *upper-shriek* functor $f^!:D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}^+(\mathcal O_Y)\to D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}^+(\mathcal O_X)$ by $f^!(K)=j^*a_{\bar f}(K)$, with the canonical identifications between compactifications. This is different in general from the unrestricted right adjoint of $Rf_*$. If $i:X\hookrightarrow Y$ is a closed immersion in $\mathrm{FTS}_S$, then for each $K\in D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}^+(\mathcal O_Y)$ there is a functorial isomorphism
\[
i^!(K)\xrightarrow{\sim}R\mathcal Hom_X(\mathcal O_X,K),
\]
where $R\mathcal Hom_X(\mathcal O_X,-)$ denotes the *exact-support* derived right adjoint to $Ri_*:D(\mathcal O_X)\to D(\mathcal O_Y)$; its pushforward is $R\mathcal Hom_{\mathcal O_Y}(i_*\mathcal O_X,K)$, and on affines $\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ with $B=A/I$ it is the sheafification of $R\operatorname{Hom}_A(B,-)$ with its natural $B$-module structure.

A first-order thickening of ringed topoi is a morphism $i:(\operatorname{Sh}(\mathcal C),\mathcal O)\to(\operatorname{Sh}(\mathcal D),\mathcal O')$ whose direct-image functor identifies the underlying topoi and whose structure-sheaf map $\mathcal O'\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal O$ is surjective with square-zero kernel $\mathcal I$. Under this identification $\mathcal I$ is an $\mathcal O$-module. A general thickening requires only a locally nilpotent kernel.

A morphism of first-order thickenings of ringed topoi $(f,f')$ is a commutative square with upper horizontal $i:(\operatorname{Sh}(\mathcal C),\mathcal O)\to(\operatorname{Sh}(\mathcal D),\mathcal O')$, lower horizontal $t:(\operatorname{Sh}(\mathcal B),\mathcal O_{\mathcal B})\to(\operatorname{Sh}(\mathcal B'),\mathcal O_{\mathcal B'})$, and vertical arrows $f,f'$. Write $\mathcal I=\ker(\mathcal O'\to\mathcal O)$ and $\mathcal J=\ker(\mathcal O_{\mathcal B'}\to\mathcal O_{\mathcal B})$. The square is strict if $(f')^*\mathcal J\to\mathcal I$ is surjective (for square-zero kernels, equivalent to $f^*\mathcal J\to\mathcal I$ being surjective).

For a first-order thickening of ringed topoi, an extension of $\mathcal O$-modules $\mathcal F,\mathcal K$ means a short exact sequence $0\to\mathcal K\to\mathcal F'\to\mathcal F\to0$ of $\mathcal O'$-modules, where $\mathcal I$ annihilates the end terms. conclusions: The descent datum glues to a quasi-coherent sheaf on $S$ and the restriction functor from $\operatorname{QCoh}(S)$ is fully faithful.
hypotheses: $S=\bigcup_iU_i$ is a Zariski open covering and $(\mathcal F_i,\phi_{ij})$ is a quasi-coherent descent datum satisfying the overlap cocycle.
theorem.statement:
Let $S$ be a scheme and $S=\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i$ an open covering. Given a family of scheme maps $\{U_i\to S\}_{i\in I}$, a descent datum for quasi-coherent sheaves is a collection of quasi-coherent $\mathcal O_{U_i}$-modules $\mathcal F_i$ with isomorphisms $\phi_{ij}:\operatorname{pr}_0^*\mathcal F_i\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{pr}_1^*\mathcal F_j$ on $U_i\times_S U_j$ satisfying the cocycle condition on every triple overlap. It is effective if the $\mathcal F_i$ are obtained, up to isomorphism of descent data, by pullback of a quasi-coherent $\mathcal O_S$-module. Then every such descent datum is effective and the canonical functor
$$\operatorname{QCoh}(S)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Desc}_{\{U_i\to S\}}(\operatorname{QCoh}),\quad\mathcal F\longmapsto(\mathcal F|_{U_i},\mathrm{can})$$
is fully faithful (indeed an equivalence of categories).

theorem.statement:
Let $\varphi : R \to S$ be a ring map.
Let $I \subset R$ be an ideal.

hypotheses: Let $f:x\to x$ be idempotent in a preadditive category, and put $g=1_x-f$; then $fg=gf=0$.
theorem.statement:
Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a preadditive category,
$x$ be an object of $\mathcal{A}$,
and $f : x \to x$ be idempotent.
Write $g = \text{id} _ x - f$
so that $f\circ g=g\circ f=0$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $f$ has kernel $i : \Ker (f) \to x$
and $p$ is the unique morphism such that $g = i \circ p$,
then $p \circ i = \text{id} _ {\Ker (f)}$
and $p$ is the cokernel of $f$.
\item If $f$ has cokernel $p : x \to \Coker (f)$
and $i$ is the unique morphism such that $g = i \circ p$,
then $p \circ i = \text{id} _ {\Coker (f)}$
and $i$ is the kernel of $f$.
\item If $g$ has kernel $j : \Ker (g) \to x$
and $q$ is the unique morphism such that $f = j \circ q$,
then $q \circ j = \text{id} _ {\Ker (g)}$
and $q$ is the cokernel of $g$.
\item If $g$ has cokernel $q : x \to \Coker (g)$
and $j$ is the unique morphism such that $f = j \circ q$,
then $q \circ j = \text{id} _ {\Coker (g)}$
and $j$ is the kernel of $g$.
\end{enumerate}

More generally, if $R\to S$ satisfies going down, then its induced spectrum map is open.
hypotheses: $R\to S$ is a unital map of commutative rings of finite presentation.
theorem.statement:
For a unital map of commutative rings $u:R\to S$, going down means: for every chain $\mathfrak p\subset\mathfrak p^\prime$ in $\operatorname{Spec}R$ and $\mathfrak q^\prime$ over $\mathfrak p^\prime$, there exists $\mathfrak q\subset\mathfrak q^\prime$ over $\mathfrak p$. Going up means: for every such chain and $\mathfrak q$ over $\mathfrak p$, there exists $\mathfrak q^\prime\supset\mathfrak q$ over $\mathfrak p^\prime$. Let $R \to S$ be flat and of finite presentation.
Then $\Spec(S) \to \Spec(R)$ is open.
More generally this holds for any ring map $R \to S$ of
finite presentation which satisfies going down.

For an étale presentation $U\to X$ by a scheme, $R=U\times_XU$ is its groupoid of arrows with projections $s,t:R\rightrightarrows U$. A morphism is representable if every base change along a map from a scheme has scheme source.

For $x\in|X|$, condition $(\alpha)_x$ means every affine étale morphism $U\to X$ has only finitely many points over $x$. Condition $(\beta)_x$ means there is a monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ representing $x$. Condition $(\gamma)_x$ means there is a quasi-compact monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ representing $x$, equivalently for every affine étale $U\to X$ both fibres over $x$ of $|U|\to|X|$ and $|U\times_XU|\to|X|$ are finite. The conditions $(\alpha),(\beta),(\gamma)$ mean the corresponding pointwise property holds at every $x$.

An algebraic space $X$ is *decent* when it satisfies $(\gamma)$, equivalently every point $x$ can be represented by a quasi-compact monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)\to X$. It is *reasonable* when it satisfies $(\delta)$, equivalently the fibres of every affine étale presentation $U\to X$ are universally bounded. It is *very reasonable* when it satisfies $(\epsilon)$, equivalently it has a Zariski-local quasi-compact surjective étale cover by schemes. The implications scheme or quasi-separated $\Rightarrow$ very reasonable $\Rightarrow$ reasonable $\Rightarrow$ decent hold.

For $x\in|X|$ and an étale morphism $U\to X$, write $(U,u)\to(X,x)$ for a pointed étale neighborhood. It is *elementary* when $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(u)\to X$ is a monomorphism representing $x$. A subset is locally constructible if its intersection with every quasi-compact open subset is a finite union of locally closed subsets. An algebraic space has a locally constructible subset in the étale sense when its inverse image in every étale scheme chart is locally constructible.

For any $S$-scheme $T$ locally of finite type, write $\delta_T(t)=\delta(f(t))+\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(f(t))}\kappa(t)$; for integral closed $W\subset T$, let $\dim_\delta W=\delta_T(\eta_W)$.

A $q$-cycle on $T$ is a locally finite integral linear combination of integral closed subschemes of $\delta$-dimension $q$; $Z_q(T)$ is the group of these cycles. For a closed subscheme $W$ of dimension at most $q$, $[W]_q$ is the sum of the $q$-dimensional components weighted by generic-point length multiplicities. The Chow group $\mathrm{CH}_q(T)$ is $Z_q(T)$ modulo rational equivalence generated by locally finite principal divisors on integral closed subschemes of dimension $q+1$.

For a morphism $f:X\to Y$ and integer $p$, a bivariant class $c\in A^p(X\to Y)$ is a collection of homomorphisms $c_T:\mathrm{CH}_q(T)\to\mathrm{CH}_{q-p}(X\times_YT)$ indexed by $T\to Y$ and $q$, satisfying: (i) for proper $h:T'\to T$, $c_T(h_*\beta)=h_{X,*}c_{T'}(\beta)$; (ii) for flat $h$ of fixed relative dimension, $c_{T'}(h^*\alpha)=h_X^*c_T(\alpha)$; (iii) for $i:E\hookrightarrow T$ the zero scheme of a section of an invertible sheaf, $c_E(i^*\alpha)=i_X^*c_T(\alpha)$, with $h_X,i_X$ the base changes. For a finite locally free sheaf $\mathcal E$ of rank $r$ on $X$, its operational Chern classes are $c_j(\mathcal E)\in A^j(X)$, with $c_0=1$, $c_j=0$ for $j>r$, and total class $c(\mathcal E)=\sum_jc_j(\mathcal E)$. theorem.title: Lemma — Proetale subcanonical

conclusions:
A ring map $A \to B$ is \'etale at a prime $\mathfrak q$ if and only if there
exists $g \in B$, $g \not \in \mathfrak q$ such that $B_g$ is standard
\'etale over $A$.
The element g avoids q and **localizes B**, not A; B_g is standard étale as defined. The two local conditions are equivalent for arbitrary ring maps and primes of B.
hypotheses:
Fix a scheme $S$. The **big $\tau$-site** $(\mathrm{Sch}/S)_\tau$ is a small-universe-selected category of $S$-schemes with covering families of type $\tau\in\{\mathrm{fppf},\mathrm{syntomic},\mathrm{smooth},\mathrm{\acute etale},\mathrm{Zariski}\}$. The **small étale site** $S_{\acute etale}$ has as objects étale $S$-schemes and as covers jointly surjective étale families; the **small Zariski site** $S_{\mathrm{Zar}}$ has open subschemes as objects. These are different sites; restriction from a big to a small site is not an identity of categories. For an abelian sheaf $\mathcal F$ on a site, $H^p_\tau(U,\mathcal F)$ denotes the $p$-th right derived functor of its sections over the site object $U$. A *standard $\tau$-cover of an affine $U$* is a **finite** jointly surjective family of affine maps $U_i\to U$, each flat finitely presented for fppf, standard syntomic, standard smooth, étale, or standard principal-open immersion, respectively.

A scheme morphism is **étale** if it is flat, locally of finite presentation and unramified, equivalently smooth of relative dimension zero. A map $A\to B$ is **standard étale** if $B\simeq(A[t]/(f))_g$, with $f\in A[t]$ monic, $g\in A[t]$ and $f'(t)$ invertible in $B$. A map $A\to B$ is étale **at** $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}B$ if $A\to B_h$ is étale for some $h\in B\setminus\mathfrak q$. An étale covering $\{U_i\to U\}$ has étale maps and jointly surjective images.

A map $A\to B$ is **standard étale** if $B\simeq(A[t]/(f))_g$, with $f\in A[t]$ monic, $g\in A[t]$ and $f'(t)$ invertible in $B$. A map $A\to B$ is étale **at** $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}B$ if $A\to B_h$ is étale for some $h\in B\setminus\mathfrak q$. An étale covering $\{U_i\to U\}$ has étale maps and jointly surjective images.

A ring map $A \to B$ is \'etale at a prime $\mathfrak q$ if and only if there
exists $g \in B$, $g \not \in \mathfrak q$ such that $B_g$ is standard
\'etale over $A$.

**Precise scope:** The element g avoids q and **localizes B**, not A; B_g is standard étale as defined. The two local conditions are equivalent for arbitrary ring maps and primes of B.

theorem.title: Lemma — Efface cohomology on closed by finite cover

conclusions: $X$ is catenary.
hypotheses: Let $S$ be a scheme and $X$ an algebraic space over $S$. Write $|X|$ for its underlying topological space, obtained from the equivalence classes of morphisms $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ from spectra of fields. The fibre product of algebraic spaces is understood in the category of algebraic spaces. For an étale presentation $U\to X$ by a scheme, $R=U\times_XU$ is its groupoid of arrows with projections $s,t:R\rightrightarrows U$. A morphism is representable if every base change along a map from a scheme has scheme source.

An algebraic space $X$ is decent if every point $x\in|X|$ admits a quasi-compact representing monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)\to X$. It is reasonable if every affine étale morphism $U\to X$ has universally bounded finite fibres, and very reasonable if it is Zariski-locally covered by quasi-compact surjective étale schemes. A morphism $f:X\to Y$ is *decent* (respectively reasonable, very reasonable or with property $(\beta)$) if $X\times_YT$ has that property for every scheme $T\to Y$. Property $(\beta)$ for a space means that every point can be represented by a monomorphism from a field spectrum.

For decent $X$ and $x\in|X|$, $\kappa(x)$ is the field associated with the representing monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)\to X$. An *elementary étale neighborhood* $(U,u)\to(X,x)$ is an étale scheme chart whose pointed field map $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(u)\to X$ is such a monomorphism. Its henselian local ring is $\mathcal O_{X,x}^{h}=\varinjlim_{(U,u)}\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U)$ over the cofiltered category of elementary étale neighborhoods, and it agrees with $\mathcal O_{U,u}^h$ for any one of them. A decent space's point-set $|X|$ is sober and admits a dense open schematic locus when it has finitely many irreducible components.

At a point $x$ of a decent algebraic space, the number of branches is the number of minimal primes of the henselian local ring $\mathcal O_{X,x}^h$, possibly infinite. The space is *unibranch at $x$* if $\mathcal O_{X,x}^h$ has precisely one minimal prime. A topological space is *catenary* if all saturated chains of specializations between fixed comparable points have the same length. A dimension function $\delta$ on a sober catenary topological space satisfies $\delta(x)=\delta(y)+1$ whenever $x\leadsto y$ is an immediate specialization. For a locally finite type map $f:X\to S$ with $S$ universally catenary carrying dimension function $\delta_S$, its induced function is $\delta_X(x)=\delta_S(f(x))+\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(f(x))}\kappa(x)$.

theorem.title: Lemma — Subsheaf of constant sheaf

conclusions: The global Gysin maps commute with the de Rham differential.
hypotheses: $Z\hookrightarrow X$ is a finitely presented closed immersion with locally free conormal of rank $c$, and $\gamma^p$ is its canonical Gysin map.
theorem.statement:
Let $X\to S$ be a morphism of schemes and $i:Z\hookrightarrow X$ a finitely presented closed immersion whose conormal sheaf $\mathcal C_{Z/X}=\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2$ is locally free of constant rank $c\geq0$. Write $\mathcal H^c_Z(-)$ for the $c$th local cohomology sheaf supported on $Z$. Locally where $Z$ is defined by $c$ functions $f_1,\ldots,f_c$, the Gysin morphism $\gamma^p:\Omega^p_{Z/S}\to\mathcal H^c_Z(\Omega^{p+c}_{X/S})$ is given by a Čech/local-cohomology class represented by $\widetilde\omega\wedge df_1\wedge\cdots\wedge df_c/(f_1\cdots f_c)$ for a local lift $\widetilde\omega$ of $\omega$.

For all $p\geq0$, the canonical global Gysin maps $\gamma^p$ commute with exterior differentiation: the square
$$\begin{array}{ccc}\Omega^p_{Z/S}&\xrightarrow{\gamma^p}&\mathcal H^c_Z(\Omega^{p+c}_{X/S})\\
\downarrow d&&\downarrow d\\
\Omega^{p+1}_{Z/S}&\xrightarrow{\gamma^{p+1}}&\mathcal H^c_Z(\Omega^{p+c+1}_{X/S})\end{array}$$
commutes.

theorem.statement:
Let $R$ be a ring. Let $n \geq m$. Let $A$ be an
$n \times m$ matrix with coefficients in $R$. Let $J \subset R$
be the ideal generated by the $m \times m$ minors of $A$.

theorem.title: Lemma — Cohomology with support quasi coherent

conclusions: The projection formula for the right adjoint holds on all unbounded quasi-coherent-derived inputs.
hypotheses: f perfect proper Noetherian, a_f right adjoint.
theorem.statement:

For every $K\in D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_Y)$, including unbounded $K$, the canonical projection-comparison morphism
\[
Lf^*K\otimes_{\mathcal O_X}^{\mathbf L}a_f(\mathcal O_Y)\xrightarrow{\sim}a_f(K)
\]
is an isomorphism. This requires perfect properness, but not flatness.

theorem.title: Lemma — Periodic determinant sign

conclusions: $\delta_X$ is a dimension function on $|X|$.
hypotheses: Let $S$ be a scheme and $X$ an algebraic space over $S$. Write $|X|$ for its underlying topological space, obtained from the equivalence classes of morphisms $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ from spectra of fields. The fibre product of algebraic spaces is understood in the category of algebraic spaces. For an étale presentation $U\to X$ by a scheme, $R=U\times_XU$ is its groupoid of arrows with projections $s,t:R\rightrightarrows U$. A morphism is representable if every base change along a map from a scheme has scheme source.

An algebraic space $X$ is decent if every point $x\in|X|$ admits a quasi-compact representing monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)\to X$. It is reasonable if every affine étale morphism $U\to X$ has universally bounded finite fibres, and very reasonable if it is Zariski-locally covered by quasi-compact surjective étale schemes. A morphism $f:X\to Y$ is *decent* (respectively reasonable, very reasonable or with property $(\beta)$) if $X\times_YT$ has that property for every scheme $T\to Y$. Property $(\beta)$ for a space means that every point can be represented by a monomorphism from a field spectrum.

For decent $X$ and $x\in|X|$, $\kappa(x)$ is the field associated with the representing monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)\to X$. An *elementary étale neighborhood* $(U,u)\to(X,x)$ is an étale scheme chart whose pointed field map $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(u)\to X$ is such a monomorphism. Its henselian local ring is $\mathcal O_{X,x}^{h}=\varinjlim_{(U,u)}\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U)$ over the cofiltered category of elementary étale neighborhoods, and it agrees with $\mathcal O_{U,u}^h$ for any one of them. A decent space's point-set $|X|$ is sober and admits a dense open schematic locus when it has finitely many irreducible components.

At a point $x$ of a decent algebraic space, the number of branches is the number of minimal primes of the henselian local ring $\mathcal O_{X,x}^h$, possibly infinite. The space is *unibranch at $x$* if $\mathcal O_{X,x}^h$ has precisely one minimal prime. A topological space is *catenary* if all saturated chains of specializations between fixed comparable points have the same length. A dimension function $\delta$ on a sober catenary topological space satisfies $\delta(x)=\delta(y)+1$ whenever $x\leadsto y$ is an immediate specialization. For a locally finite type map $f:X\to S$ with $S$ universally catenary carrying dimension function $\delta_S$, its induced function is $\delta_X(x)=\delta_S(f(x))+\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(f(x))}\kappa(x)$.

theorem.statement: Let $D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_T)$ be the unbounded derived category of complexes of $\mathcal O_T$-modules having quasi-coherent cohomology sheaves. theorem.title: Lemma — Image connected space

conclusions: Every τ descent datum of P-type schemes is effective.
hypotheses: P is base-change stable, finite-coproduct stable, and affine-singleton descent effective for the indicated τ-coverings.
theorem.statement:
Let $\mathcal P$ be a property of morphisms of schemes over a base, and let $\tau\in\{\mathrm{fpqc},\mathrm{fppf},\mathrm{\acute etale},\mathrm{smooth},\mathrm{syntomic}\}$. Say that *morphisms of type $\mathcal P$ satisfy descent for $\tau$-coverings* if, for every $\tau$-covering $\{U_i\to S\}$, every scheme descent datum $(X_i,\varphi_{ij})$ with each $X_i\to U_i$ having $\mathcal P$ is effective, i.e. isomorphic to the canonical pullback descent datum of some $S$-scheme.

Suppose (1) $\mathcal P$ is preserved by arbitrary base change; (2) $\mathcal P$ is preserved by finite disjoint unions of morphisms, so that if $Y_j\to V_j$ have $\mathcal P$ for $1\leq j\leq m$, then $\coprod_jY_j\to\coprod_jV_j$ has $\mathcal P$; and (3) for each surjective map of affine schemes $X\to S$ of the corresponding class—flat for fpqc, flat and of finite presentation for fppf, étale for étale, smooth for smooth, and syntomic for syntomic—every descent datum $(V,\varphi)$ for $X/S$ with $V\to X$ having $\mathcal P$ is effective. Then morphisms of type $\mathcal P$ satisfy descent for all $\tau$-coverings. This asserts effectivity of the descent datum; the definition does not separately assert that its descended morphism has $\mathcal P$.

Morphisms are $X$-morphisms compatible with these isomorphisms. For a morphism $f:X'\to X$ over $S$, pullback is the functor $f^*:\mathrm{DD}(X/S)\to\mathrm{DD}(X'/S)$ taking $V$ to $V\times_X X'$ and $\varphi$ to its pullback along $f\times_Sf$. If $f:X\to X$ is any morphism over $S$, then $f^*:\mathrm{DD}(X/S)\to\mathrm{DD}(X/S)$ is naturally isomorphic to the identity functor. theorem.title: Lemma — Coherent projective

conclusions: $X$ is a scheme.
$X \cong \Spec(k)$ for some field $k$.
hypotheses: Let $S$ be a scheme and $X$ an algebraic space over $S$. Write $|X|$ for its underlying topological space, obtained from the equivalence classes of morphisms $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ from spectra of fields. The fibre product of algebraic spaces is understood in the category of algebraic spaces. For an étale presentation $U\to X$ by a scheme, $R=U\times_XU$ is its groupoid of arrows with projections $s,t:R\rightrightarrows U$. A morphism is representable if every base change along a map from a scheme has scheme source.

For $x\in|X|$, condition $(\alpha)_x$ means every affine étale morphism $U\to X$ has only finitely many points over $x$. Condition $(\beta)_x$ means there is a monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ representing $x$. Condition $(\gamma)_x$ means there is a quasi-compact monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ representing $x$, equivalently for every affine étale $U\to X$ both fibres over $x$ of $|U|\to|X|$ and $|U\times_XU|\to|X|$ are finite. The conditions $(\alpha),(\beta),(\gamma)$ mean the corresponding pointwise property holds at every $x$.

An algebraic space $X$ is *decent* when it satisfies $(\gamma)$, equivalently every point $x$ can be represented by a quasi-compact monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)\to X$. It is *reasonable* when it satisfies $(\delta)$, equivalently the fibres of every affine étale presentation $U\to X$ are universally bounded. It is *very reasonable* when it satisfies $(\epsilon)$, equivalently it has a Zariski-local quasi-compact surjective étale cover by schemes. The implications scheme or quasi-separated $\Rightarrow$ very reasonable $\Rightarrow$ reasonable $\Rightarrow$ decent hold.

A *residual space* $Z_x\to X$ at $x\in|X|$ is the unique monomorphism from a reduced locally Noetherian algebraic space with singleton underlying topology whose image is $x$ and which is universal among morphisms of such spaces into $X$ representing $x$. A space is *locally separated* if its diagonal is an immersion; it is quasi-separated if its diagonal is quasi-compact and quasi-separated. A locally Noetherian algebraic space is one with an étale cover by locally Noetherian schemes.

For points $a,b$ of a topological space, $b\leadsto a$ means $a\in\overline{\{b\}}$, i.e., $a$ is a specialization of $b$. The space is $T_0$ (Kolmogorov) when distinct points have distinct closures, and sober when every irreducible closed subset has exactly one generic point. A subset is locally constructible if its intersection with every quasi-compact open subset is a finite union of locally closed subsets. An algebraic space has a locally constructible subset in the étale sense when its inverse image in every étale scheme chart is locally constructible.
theorem.statement:
Let $S$ be a scheme and $X$ an algebraic space over $S$. Write $|X|$ for its underlying topological space, obtained from the equivalence classes of morphisms $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ from spectra of fields. The fibre product of algebraic spaces is understood in the category of algebraic spaces. For an étale presentation $U\to X$ by a scheme, $R=U\times_XU$ is its groupoid of arrows with projections $s,t:R\rightrightarrows U$. A morphism is representable if every base change along a map from a scheme has scheme source.

For $x\in|X|$, condition $(\alpha)_x$ means every affine étale morphism $U\to X$ has only finitely many points over $x$. Condition $(\beta)_x$ means there is a monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ representing $x$. Condition $(\gamma)_x$ means there is a quasi-compact monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ representing $x$, equivalently for every affine étale $U\to X$ both fibres over $x$ of $|U|\to|X|$ and $|U\times_XU|\to|X|$ are finite. The conditions $(\alpha),(\beta),(\gamma)$ mean the corresponding pointwise property holds at every $x$.

An algebraic space $X$ is *decent* when it satisfies $(\gamma)$, equivalently every point $x$ can be represented by a quasi-compact monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)\to X$. It is *reasonable* when it satisfies $(\delta)$, equivalently the fibres of every affine étale presentation $U\to X$ are universally bounded. It is *very reasonable* when it satisfies $(\epsilon)$, equivalently it has a Zariski-local quasi-compact surjective étale cover by schemes. The implications scheme or quasi-separated $\Rightarrow$ very reasonable $\Rightarrow$ reasonable $\Rightarrow$ decent hold.

A *residual space* $Z_x\to X$ at $x\in|X|$ is the unique monomorphism from a reduced locally Noetherian algebraic space with singleton underlying topology whose image is $x$ and which is universal among morphisms of such spaces into $X$ representing $x$. A space is *locally separated* if its diagonal is an immersion; it is quasi-separated if its diagonal is quasi-compact and quasi-separated. A locally Noetherian algebraic space is one with an étale cover by locally Noetherian schemes.

For points $a,b$ of a topological space, $b\leadsto a$ means $a\in\overline{\{b\}}$, i.e., $a$ is a specialization of $b$. The space is $T_0$ (Kolmogorov) when distinct points have distinct closures, and sober when every irreducible closed subset has exactly one generic point. A subset is locally constructible if its intersection with every quasi-compact open subset is a finite union of locally closed subsets. An algebraic space has a locally constructible subset in the étale sense when its inverse image in every étale scheme chart is locally constructible.

Let $S$ be a scheme. Let $X$ be a decent algebraic space over $S$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $|X|$ is a singleton then $X$ is a scheme.
\item If $|X|$ is a singleton and $X$ is reduced, then
$X \cong \operatorname{Spec}(k)$ for some field $k$.
\end{enumerate}

A dualizing complex $\omega_A^\bullet$ over a Noetherian ring is a bounded coherent complex of finite injective dimension with $A\simeq R\operatorname{Hom}_A(\omega_A^\bullet,\omega_A^\bullet)$. Let $(A, \mathfrak m, \kappa)$ be a Noetherian local ring
with normalized dualizing complex $\omega_A^\bullet$
and dualizing module $\omega_A = H^{-\dim(A)}(\omega_A^\bullet)$.
The following are equivalent
\begin{enumerate}
\item $A$ is Cohen-Macaulay,
\item $\omega_A^\bullet$ is concentrated in a single degree, and
\item $\omega_A^\bullet = \omega_A[\dim(A)]$.
\end{enumerate}
In this case $\omega_A$ is a maximal Cohen-Macaulay module.

A maximal Cohen–Macaulay module has depth equal to dim A.

theorem.statement:
Fix a Noetherian base $S$. Write $\mathrm{FTS}_S$ for separated schemes of finite type over $S$, with $S$-morphisms. For $f:X\to Y$ in $\mathrm{FTS}_S$, choose a factorization $f=\bar f\circ j$ with $j:X\hookrightarrow\bar X$ an open immersion and $\bar f:\bar X\to Y$ proper. If $a_{\bar f}$ is the right adjoint to $R\bar f_*$ on unbounded quasi-coherent derived categories, define $f^!:D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}^+(\mathcal O_Y)\to D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}^+(\mathcal O_X)$ as $j^*a_{\bar f}$, independently (up to canonical identifications) of the chosen compactification. For a dualizing complex $D_T$ on a locally Noetherian scheme $T$, its associated dimension function $\delta_T:T\to\mathbf Z$ assigns to $t$ the unique integer such that the stalk $D_{T,t}[-\delta_T(t)]$ is a *normalized* dualizing complex over $\mathcal O_{T,t}$, i.e. $R\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_{T,t}}(\kappa(t),D_{T,t}[-\delta_T(t)])\simeq\kappa(t)[0]$. For $x\in X$ above $y\in Y$, let $X_y=X\times_Y\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(y)$ be the fibre and $\dim_x(X_y)$ its local topological dimension at $x$ (minimum dimension of neighbourhoods in the fibre). Let $x\in X$, $y=f(x)$. If $H^i(f^!\mathcal O_Y)_x$ is nonzero, then
\[
i\ge-\dim_x(X_y).
\]
This is a lower bound for degrees of the upper-shriek structure complex; without extra hypotheses there is no asserted universal upper bound.

Let $S$ be locally Noetherian and universally catenary with dimension function $\delta:S\to\mathbf Z$. For $X$ locally of finite type over $S$, $\delta_X(x)=\delta(f(x))+\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(f(x))}\kappa(x)$; $\dim_\delta(W)$ is its value at the generic point of integral $W$.

$Z_k(X)$ is the group of locally finite integer combinations of integral closed subschemes of $\delta$-dimension $k$. The cycle $[Z]_k$ of a closed subscheme $Z$ of dimension at most $k$ sums its $k$-dimensional components weighted by generic-point stalk lengths; $[\mathcal F]_k$ uses lengths of a coherent sheaf at the corresponding generic points of its support.

For a proper map $f:X\to Y$, $f_*[W]=0$ if $\dim_\delta f(W)<\dim_\delta W$, otherwise it is $[\kappa(\eta_W):\kappa(\eta_{f(W)})][f(W)]$. $\mathrm{CH}_k(X)=Z_k(X)/\!\sim_{\mathrm{rat}}$, where rational equivalence is generated by locally finite sums of principal divisors of nonzero rational functions on integral closed subschemes of dimension $k+1$, pushed into $X$. An envelope is a proper map $f:Y\to X$ such that every $x\in X$ has some $y$ above it with $\kappa(y)\simeq\kappa(x)$.

Let $X$ be a scheme locally of finite type over $S$.
If $f : Y \to X$ and $g : Z \to Y$ are envelopes, then
$f \circ g$ is an envelope.

theorem.title: Lemma — Locally projective pushforward

conclusions: Derived Hom comparison and all Ext^i base-change maps are isomorphisms.
hypotheses: A→B flat with A/I≈B/IB; K torsion-cohomology and L arbitrary.
theorem.statement:
Let $A$ be a commutative ring, $I=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\subseteq A$ finitely generated, and $Z=V(I)\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}A$. Let $D_{\mathcal T_I}(A)\subseteq D(A)$ be the full triangulated subcategory of complexes whose cohomology modules are $I$-power torsion. Let $C_A(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ be the *augmented alternating Čech complex* $[A\to\bigoplus_i A_{f_i}\to\bigoplus_{i<j}A_{f_if_j}\to\cdots\to A_{f_1\cdots f_r}]$, with $A$ in degree $0$, the standard alternating restriction differentials, and all terms flat. Define $R\Gamma_Z(K)=C_A(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\otimes_A^{\mathbf L}K\in D_{\mathcal T_I}(A)$, the right adjoint to the inclusion $D_{\mathcal T_I}(A)\hookrightarrow D(A)$. This is local cohomology, unlike $R\Gamma_I$ above for general non-Noetherian $A$. Let $A\to B$ be flat with $A/I\xrightarrow{\sim}B/IB$. If $K\in D_{\mathcal T_I}(A)$ and $L\in D(A)$, then the canonical map
\[
R\operatorname{Hom}_A(K,L)\xrightarrow{\sim}R\operatorname{Hom}_B(K\otimes_AB,L\otimes_AB)
\]
is a quasi-isomorphism of underlying derived complexes of abelian groups (equivalently of $A$-modules by restriction on the right). In particular, for $A$-modules $M,N$ with $M$ $I$-power torsion, $\operatorname{Ext}_A^i(M,N)\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Ext}_B^i(M\otimes_AB,N\otimes_AB)$ for every $i\ge0$. Flatness allows ordinary tensor rather than derived tensor on modules.

theorem.title: Theorem — Injective embedding grothendieck

conclusions: Gorenstein at x iff f^!O_Y derived-invertible around x; locus open.
hypotheses: f flat in FTS_S, x∈X.
theorem.statement: A *Gorenstein local ring* is a Noetherian local ring of finite injective dimension as a module over itself; a scheme $T$ is *Gorenstein* if it is locally Noetherian and all its local rings are Gorenstein. A complex in $D(\mathcal O_T)$ is *derived-invertible* if it has a two-sided derived tensor inverse, equivalently it is locally a shift of a line bundle. For a scheme morphism $f:X\to Y$ whose fibres are locally Noetherian, *Gorenstein at $x$* means that $f$ is flat at $x$ and the local ring of $X_{f(x)}$ at $x$ is Gorenstein; *Gorenstein morphism* means this condition at every point. Fix a Noetherian scheme $S$ and the category $\mathrm{FTS}_S$ of separated finite-type $S$-schemes. For $f:X\to Y$ therein, let $f^!:D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}^+(\mathcal O_Y)\to D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}^+(\mathcal O_X)$ be the upper-shriek functor built from the right adjoint to proper pushforward on a compactification $X\hookrightarrow\bar X\to Y$. In particular $f^!\mathcal O_Y$ is a coherent bounded complex when $f$ is perfect. Let $f:X\to Y$ be flat in $\mathrm{FTS}_S$ and $x\in X$. Then $f$ is Gorenstein at $x$ iff there exists an open neighbourhood $U\subseteq X$ of $x$ on which $f^!\mathcal O_Y|_U$ is **derived-invertible**, i.e. locally isomorphic to a shift of a line bundle. In particular the pointwise Gorenstein locus is open. This relative criterion uses the upper-shriek *complex*, not just its zeroth cohomology.

theorem.statement:
Fix a prime $p$ and a divided power scheme $(S,\mathcal I,\gamma)$ over $\mathbf Z_{(p)}$, where $\mathcal I$ is a quasi-coherent ideal with divided powers. Set $S_0=V(\mathcal I)$ and choose a morphism $X\to S_0$ on which $p$ is locally nilpotent. A divided power thickening of $X/S$ is a triple $(U,T,\delta)$ with a closed immersion $U\hookrightarrow T$ inducing a homeomorphism on topological spaces, divided powers $\delta$ on its ideal $\mathcal J_T$, a compatible morphism of divided power schemes $T\to S$, and a map $U\to X$. These objects with compatible maps form $\mathrm{CRIS}(X/S)$; its full subcategory $\mathrm{Cris}(X/S)$ has $U\to X$ an open immersion. Both carry the Zariski topology (covers arise from Zariski covers of $T$ compatible with $U$). The forgetful functor $\mathrm{CRIS}(X/S)\to\operatorname{Sch}/X$ sends $(U,T,\delta)$ to $U$.

On the small crystalline site $\mathrm{Cris}(X/S)$, the crystalline structure sheaf $\mathcal O_{X/S}$ restricts to $\mathcal O_T$ on an object $(U,T,\delta)$. A sheaf $\mathcal F$ of $\mathcal O_{X/S}$-modules restricts to a sheaf $\mathcal F_T$ on $T$. It is a crystal if each pullback comparison map $f^*\mathcal F_T\to\mathcal F_{T'}$ for a morphism $(U',T',\delta')\to(U,T,\delta)$ is an isomorphism. It is locally quasi-coherent if every $\mathcal F_T$ is quasi-coherent, and quasi-coherent as a module on the site if it is locally presented by free $\mathcal O_{X/S}$-modules. The sheaf $\Omega_{X/S}$ is the universal divided power sheaf of differentials for the structure morphism of the crystalline site to the Zariski site of $S$; it restricts to $\Omega_{T/S,\delta}$ on each object.

Under the global crystalline setup above, let $\mathcal C=\mathrm{Cris}(X/S)$ or $\mathrm{CRIS}(X/S)$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of $\mathcal O_{X/S}$-modules on $\mathcal C$. The following are equivalent
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\mathcal{F}$ is quasi-coherent, and
\item $\mathcal{F}$ is locally quasi-coherent and a crystal in
$\mathcal{O}_{X/S}$-modules.
\end{enumerate}

For a ring map $A\to B$, let $\Omega_{B/A}$ be the module of Kähler differentials. The cotangent complex $L_{B/A}\in D(B)$ is obtained from the standard augmented simplicial polynomial $A$-algebra resolution $P_\bullet\to B$, where $P_0=A[B]$, $P_1=A[A[B]]$, etc., by taking the chain complex (in nonpositive cohomological degrees) associated to the simplicial $B$-module $\Omega_{P_\bullet/A}\otimes_{P_\bullet}B$. Here $A[E]$ denotes the polynomial algebra freely generated by a set $E$, $D(B)$ is the derived category of $B$-modules, and $H^i$ denotes degree-$i$ cohomology.

A quasi-isomorphism is a map of complexes inducing an isomorphism on every cohomology module. We write $M[0]$ for a module concentrated in degree zero, $M[1]$ for a module in degree $-1$, $\otimes_A^{\mathbf L}$ for derived tensor product, and $\tau_{\geq -1}$ for the standard truncation in cohomological degrees at least $-1$. The module $\Omega_{B/A}$ is generated by symbols $db$ subject to additivity, the Leibniz rule, and $da=0$ for $a\in A$.

For a directed system of ring maps $(A_i\to B_i)$, let $A=\varinjlim A_i$ and $B=\varinjlim B_i$. When comparing $L_{B_i/A_i}$ over the different rings $B_i$, use the transition maps to view their filtered colimit as a complex over $B$. Filtered colimits of modules are exact and commute with polynomial algebra formation and Kähler differentials.

Let $A_i \to B_i$ be a system of ring maps over a directed index
set $I$. Then, with the filtered colimit taken using the functorial transition maps and viewed as a complex of $\varinjlim B_i$-modules, $\varinjlim_i L_{B_i/A_i}\simeq L_{\varinjlim_i B_i/\varinjlim_i A_i}$.

hypotheses: Let $S$ be a scheme and $X$ an algebraic space over $S$. Write $|X|$ for its underlying topological space, obtained from the equivalence classes of morphisms $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ from spectra of fields. The fibre product of algebraic spaces is understood in the category of algebraic spaces. For an étale presentation $U\to X$ by a scheme, $R=U\times_XU$ is its groupoid of arrows with projections $s,t:R\rightrightarrows U$. A morphism is representable if every base change along a map from a scheme has scheme source.

For $x\in|X|$, condition $(\alpha)_x$ means every affine étale morphism $U\to X$ has only finitely many points over $x$. Condition $(\beta)_x$ means there is a monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ representing $x$. Condition $(\gamma)_x$ means there is a quasi-compact monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ representing $x$, equivalently for every affine étale $U\to X$ both fibres over $x$ of $|U|\to|X|$ and $|U\times_XU|\to|X|$ are finite. The conditions $(\alpha),(\beta),(\gamma)$ mean the corresponding pointwise property holds at every $x$.

An algebraic space $X$ is *decent* when it satisfies $(\gamma)$, equivalently every point $x$ can be represented by a quasi-compact monomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)\to X$. It is *reasonable* when it satisfies $(\delta)$, equivalently the fibres of every affine étale presentation $U\to X$ are universally bounded. It is *very reasonable* when it satisfies $(\epsilon)$, equivalently it has a Zariski-local quasi-compact surjective étale cover by schemes. The implications scheme or quasi-separated $\Rightarrow$ very reasonable $\Rightarrow$ reasonable $\Rightarrow$ decent hold.

A *residual space* $Z_x\to X$ at $x\in|X|$ is the unique monomorphism from a reduced locally Noetherian algebraic space with singleton underlying topology whose image is $x$ and which is universal among morphisms of such spaces into $X$ representing $x$. A space is *locally separated* if its diagonal is an immersion; it is quasi-separated if its diagonal is quasi-compact and quasi-separated. A locally Noetherian algebraic space is one with an étale cover by locally Noetherian schemes.

theorem.statement:
For a proper $k$-scheme $X$ of dimension $1$ with $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X)=k$, its genus is $g(X)=\dim_kH^1(X,\mathcal O_X)$ and $\chi(X,\mathcal O_X)=1-g(X)$. Let $X$ be a proper curve over a field $k$ with $H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X) = k$.

theorem.statement:
Let $X \to T \to S$ be morphisms of schemes with $T \to S$ \'etale.
Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a quasi-coherent $\mathcal{O}_X$-module.
Let $x \in X$ be a point. Then
$$
\mathcal{F}\text{ flat over }S\text{ at }x
\Leftrightarrow
\mathcal{F}\text{ flat over }T\text{ at }x
$$
In particular $\mathcal{F}$ is flat over $S$ if and only if $\mathcal{F}$
is flat over $T$.
